lesson.title: The Latin Bridge (-ieren)
lesson.subtitle: Unlock 500+ German verbs instantly with the Romance loan suffix

hook.title: The Medieval Aristocratic Cheat Code
hook.content: During the High Middle Ages, French courtly culture swept across European nobility. German knights and scholars borrowed hundreds of French verbs ending in '-ier'. To assimilate them into German grammar, they welded the native Germanic infinitive ending '-en' onto the French suffix, creating '-ieren' (-ier + -en). Because English borrowed the exact same Latin roots after the Norman Conquest, you instantly understand hundreds of advanced German verbs!

footnotes.title: Old French -ier + Germanic -en
footnotes.content: Originating in 12th-century Middle High German courtly poetry, this hybrid suffix became the universal German receptor for international loan verbs.

pattern.title: The -ieren Formula & The No-'ge-' Secret
pattern.content: Any English intellectual, technical, or Latinate verb ending in -ate, -ize, or -ify maps to a German -ieren verb (-ize and -ify add -is- or -ifiz- before -ieren: organisieren, klassifizieren): study ↔ studieren, repair ↔ reparieren, organize ↔ organisieren, function ↔ funktionieren, grasp ↔ kapieren (from Latin capere), accept ↔ akzeptieren, and reserve ↔ reservieren. Unlike Germanic verbs, verbs in -ieren always stress the suffix (stu-DIE-ren). Because German phonotactics rejects the prefix 'ge-' on verbs without initial root stress, -ieren verbs NEVER take 'ge-' in the past participle: studiert, repariert, funktioniert!

footnotes.title: Stress and Participle Rules
footnotes.content: Suffix stress (/iːʁən/) prohibits unaccented 'ge-' in the Perfekt participle (studiert, NOT gestudiert).

exercises.prompt: Assemble the German verb for 'to organize' (Latin root + romance infinitive):
Match the English Latinate verbs with their German -ieren counterparts:
exercises.target_answer: studieren, reparieren, funktionieren, kapieren, akzeptieren, informieren, existieren
exercises.meaning: to study, to repair, to function, to grasp, to accept, to inform, to exist
exercises.explanation: French/Latin verbs entered English directly and entered German through the -ieren suffix — accept, inform and exist included.

exercises.prompt: Why do verbs ending in '-ieren' never take the prefix 'ge-' in the past participle (e.g. studiert, NOT gestudiert)?
options: Because they are borrowed from English
Because they are irregular strong verbs
The stress is on the suffix (-IE-ren), and German only adds 'ge-' to verbs with root stress
exercises.target_answer: The stress is on the suffix (-IE-ren), and German only adds 'ge-' to verbs with root stress
exercises.explanation: German past participle prefix ge- attaches only to verbs with initial syllable stress. Since -ieren shifts stress to the suffix, ge- is phonetically rejected.

exercises.prompt: Apply the -ieren rule: English 'to repair' → German verb:

exercises.idea: you're annoyed at the café: the computer doesn't work
cues: Der Computer is the subject; the -ieren verb takes position 2, conjugated: funktioniert (-ier stem + the er/sie/es -t)
Negation lands at the end: nicht — the no-thing word (not ↔ nicht: gh became ch)
exercises.explanation: Subject, conjugated -ieren verb in position 2, nicht at the end — the Romance stamp never changes, only the personal ending does.

diagnosis.slip: the -ieren verb stayed in dictionary clothes
diagnosis.cue: Position 2 needs the conjugated form: funktioniert (-ier + the er/sie/es -t). The stamp -ieren is for the dictionary, not the sentence.

summary.outcome: Recognize common German verbs ending in -ieren and use one in a simple statement.
summary.takeaway: Romance loan verbs systematically end in '-ieren', carry suffix stress, and drop 'ge-' in the past participle.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the -ieren verb builder — copy becomes kopieren, produce becomes produzieren: one stamp, five hundred verbs.

twist.prompt: Turn the -ieren verb on yourself: he studies → I study. What happens to the ending? (Careful — ich keeps an -e.)
twist.explanation: funktioniert was the er-form (-t); for ich it's studiere (-e). The Romance stamp -ieren never moves — only the personal ending does. And studieren takes its object bare: Ich studiere Deutsch.

reparieren.context_translation: I have to repair the television.

funktionieren.etymology_derivation: Used specifically for machines and mechanisms functioning properly.

kapieren.context_translation: Did you get it / grasp it?
kapieren.etymology_derivation: From Latin capere (to seize/capture). Mental grasp.

akzeptieren.etymology_derivation: Latin acceptare (hard c → k, soft c → z [ts]).

reservieren.context_translation: I would like to reserve a table.

existieren.context_translation: The problem does not exist anymore.

rock.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hrukkaz; English skirt is from a different root — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

feuer.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *fuir, PIE *péh₂wr̥ — English fire is the explicit cognate (see Feuerzeug). [wiktionary]

gewürz.context_phrase: Diese Suppe braucht noch ein Gewürz.
gewürz.context_translation: This soup needs one more spice.
gewürz.etymology_derivation: Gewürz — a 14th-century collective of Wurz (wort, herb, root), compared by Wiktionary with English wort; spices are literally the old herbs. [wiktionary]

sanft.context_phrase: Die Musik ist sanft und leise.
sanft.context_translation: The music is gentle and quiet.
sanft.etymology_derivation: West Germanic *samft(ī) — the page lists soft as the only English cognate; the root may reach back to *sem- 'one'. [wiktionary]

wurm.etymology_derivation: From Old High German wurm, from Proto-Germanic *wurmiz, from PIE *wr̥mis. English worm is the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

ärgern.etymology_derivation: From arg, bad — the page compares English eerie, its cousin from the same Germanic root for fearful. [wiktionary]

schieben.context_phrase: Wir schieben den Wagen von Hand.
schieben.context_translation: We push the car by hand.
schieben.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *skeubaną (PIE *skewbʰ-) — English shove is the documented cognate; strong verb: schob, geschoben. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
